Chapter 2

Understanding Your Role

理解你的角色

In Chapter 1, we dove into the chaos, where unpredictability dominates and engineering leaders like you are tasked with navigating the storm. The stakes are high, but so are the opportunities if you can guide your team through the turbulence.

在第 1 章里，我们一头扎进了混乱之中——在那里，不可预测性占据主导，而像你这样的工程领导者，任务就是驾船穿越风暴。赌注很高，但只要你能带领团队闯过风浪，回报也同样丰厚。

But before leading anyone, you must be clear on your role. In chaotic environments, things move fast, plans shift, and roadmaps are often missing. Your job is to create clarity, build stability, and keep your team anchored, even when everything around you is shifting.

但在带领任何人之前，你必须先想清楚自己的角色。在混乱的环境里，一切都在快速变动，计划不断调整，路线图常常根本不存在。你的工作就是：哪怕周围一切都在漂移，也要创造清晰、建立稳定、让团队稳住锚点。

It’s not just about coding or managing tasks; it’s about setting direction when none exists, creating cohesion out of chaos, and ensuring your engineers are connected to the bigger picture. And sometimes, even that picture is a little blurry.

这不仅仅是写代码或管任务；而是在没有方向时给出方向，从混乱中凝聚共识，并确保你的工程师与全局图景相连。而且有时候，就连那幅全局图景本身也有点模糊。

In this chapter, we’ll define what your role really is. You’ll map out your core responsibilities and learn how to lead effectively when the rules keep changing. Consider this your onboarding guide to the role. Whether you’re at a scrappy startup or a rapidly evolving enterprise, the foundation of your leadership remains the same: your people, your mission, your plan, your process, and your product.

在本章中，我们会定义你的角色究竟是什么。你将梳理自己的核心职责，并学会在规则不断变化时如何有效领导。把这一章当作你这个岗位的入职指南。无论你身处一家拼劲十足的初创公司，还是一家快速演进的大型企业，你领导力的根基始终是同一套：你的人（people）、你的使命（mission）、你的计划（plan）、你的流程（process）、你的产品（product）。

What’s Your Job, Exactly?

你到底是干什么的？

When you leaped into leadership, it might have felt simple: lead a team and ship great code. Easy, right? But here’s the reality: leading a team is far more than meeting deadlines. You’ll wear a thousand hats in chaotic environments, often on the same day. You’ll be a people leader, a technical guide, a strategist, a product manager, a firefighter, and sometimes a therapist. The real challenge isn’t just balancing these responsibilities; it’s knowing when to wear each hat and how to keep everything moving forward.

当你纵身跃入领导岗时，事情看起来或许很简单：带好团队、交付优秀代码。容易吧？但现实是：带团队远不止是赶截止日期。在混乱的环境里，你一天之内就要换一千顶帽子：你是人的领导、技术向导、战略家、产品经理、救火队员，有时还得当心理疏导师。真正的挑战不只是平衡这些职责，而是知道何时该戴哪顶帽子、以及如何让一切持续向前运转。

— 原书第 33 页 —

Think about it like this: your role as an engineering leader is the glue that holds everything together. You’re ensuring that your team isn’t just working in isolation but building something that matters. And here’s the secret: your team will mirror you. If you’re confused, they’ll be lost. If you’re clear, they’ll find clarity too.

可以这样理解：你作为工程领导者的角色，就是把一切粘在一起的那股胶水。你要确保团队不是各自为战地干活，而是在一起构建有意义的东西。这里有个秘密：你的团队会像镜子一样照出你自己。如果你困惑，他们就会迷茫；如果你清晰，他们也会找到清晰。

The good news is that you don’t need all the answers. You just need to build the framework, the core pillars that ground your leadership. We will break this down into five critical areas that define your job as an engineering leader, each essential to creating order from chaos: people, mission, plan, process, and product (as shown in Figure 2-1). We’ll use each of these pillars to address the symptoms of chaos we described in Chapter 1.

好消息是：你不需要掌握所有答案。你只需要搭起那个框架——那几根支撑你领导力的核心支柱。我们会把它拆解为定义工程领导工作的五个关键领域，每一个对于从混乱中建立秩序都不可或缺：人、使命、计划、流程、产品（如图 2-1 所示）。我们会用这五根支柱，逐一应对第 1 章里描述过的那些混乱症状。

Table 2-1 summarizes the critical areas shown in Figure 2-1.

The Five Pillars of Engineering Leadership

工程领导力的五大支柱

At its core, your role can be distilled into five key pillars. Master these, and you’ll have the foundation you need to thrive, no matter how chaotic your environment is:

从根本上说，你的角色可以提炼为五根关键支柱。把这五根支柱吃透，无论环境多么混乱，你都拥有了茁壮成长所需的根基：

People. Everything starts with your team. Without them, you’re not leading anyone. But it’s not just about managing a headcount. You’re responsible for building a culture, supporting growth, and ensuring that engineers work together as a unit, not just as individual contributors.

人（People）。一切都从你的团队开始。没有他们，你就没有可领导的对象。但这不仅仅是管理人员数量。你要负责打造文化、支持成长，并确保工程师们作为一个整体协作，而不只是各自为战的个体贡献者。

Mission. Why is your team building what they’re building? The mission is the “why” that drives your team forward. It’s your job to connect the dots between what your engineers are doing and the bigger picture—how their work ties into the company’s goals and what their impact is.

使命（Mission）。你的团队为什么要做他们正在做的事？使命就是驱动团队向前的那个“为什么”。你的工作是把工程师正在做的事和全局图景连成线——他们的工作如何与公司目标挂钩、他们产生的影响是什么。

Plan. Once the mission is clear, you must figure out how to get there. This is where you lay out the roadmap, prioritize work, and delegate effectively. Rather than dictating every detail, a plan should be about giving your team the direction and focus they need to move forward confidently.

计划（Plan）。使命一旦清晰，你就必须搞清楚怎么到达那里。在这一步，你要铺路线图、排优先级、有效授权。好的计划不是事无巨细地下命令，而是给团队指明方向、让他们能充满信心地向前走。

Process. A great plan is only helpful with the right processes to keep things moving. Process is what enables your team to work efficiently and stay on track. But here’s the thing: ineffective processes will destroy progress. Your job is to set up processes that support your engineers, not bog them down.

流程（Process）。再好的计划，也需要配套的正确流程才能落地。流程让团队高效协作、不走偏。但要注意：低效的流程会摧毁进展。你的工作是建立能托举工程师的流程，而不是把他们拖垮。

Product. Finally, consider what you are delivering. It’s not enough to ship features; you must ensure that your team delivers outcomes that matter. Whether it’s a feature, a fix, or an internal tool, everything your team does should have a measurable impact.

产品（Product）。最后，要想清楚你到底在交付什么。仅仅交付功能是不够的；你必须确保团队交付的是有价值的结果。无论是一个功能、一个修复，还是一个内部工具，团队做的每一件事都应产生可衡量的影响。

Boss, Where’s the Roadmap?

老板，路线图在哪儿？

So, how do we determine where we stand? Let’s face it: most of us didn’t step into leadership with a neatly defined job description that maps out every responsibility and tells us precisely what to do. More often than not, we’re handed a vague mandate to “lead the team” and are left to figure out the rest.

那么，我们怎么判断自己所处的位置？说实话：我们大多数人走上领导岗时，手里并没有一份写得清清楚楚、把每项职责都列明白、精确告诉我们该做什么的岗位说明书。更多时候，我们拿到的只是一句含糊的指令——“去带好这个团队”——然后剩下的全靠自己琢磨。

But the truth is, even if you had a detailed job description, it probably wouldn’t survive the first month on the job. Why? Because leadership, especially in chaotic environments, isn’t static. Your responsibilities will shift and evolve as the organization grows—priorities change and new challenges will emerge.

但真相是：即便你真有一份详尽的岗位说明书，它大概也撑不过入职头一个月。为什么？因为领导力——尤其是在混乱环境里——从来不是静态的。随着组织成长，你的职责会不断变化、演进——优先级在变，新的挑战也会不断冒出来。

— 原书第 35 页 —

That’s why defining your role is so critical. You need a living document that outlines your responsibilities and how you plan to fulfill them—an adaptable document, just like you.

这就是为什么定义自己的角色如此关键。你需要一份“活的文件”，写清你的职责以及你打算如何履行它们——一份像你自己一样可调整的文件。

Don’t Retreat to the Comfortable

不要躲回舒适区

Here’s the temptation: when chaos arrives, you might want to retreat into what’s comfortable or, worse, be frozen with inaction. For many of us, that means diving back into the technical work—refactoring or fixing bugs ourselves—because that’s what we know. But the hard truth is that this is not your job anymore. If you’re constantly doing the work of individual contributors, you’re not leading; you’re hiding.

诱惑就在这里：混乱一来，你可能想缩回让自己舒服的事情里去，更糟的情况是干脆僵在原地不动。对我们很多人来说，那意味着一头扎回技术活里——自己动手重构、修 bug——因为那是我们熟悉的。但残酷的真相是：这已经不是你的工作了。如果你一直在干个体贡献者的活，那你不是在领导，你是在躲。

As an engineering leader, your value is in how well you empower your team to succeed. And that means letting go of the need to be the technical expert in every situation. Your job is to guide, to enable, and to steer, rather than to do everything yourself. Leading engineers is not a promotion; it’s a whole new job.

作为工程领导者，你的价值在于你能在多大程度上赋能团队取得成功。这意味着你要放下“在任何场景下都必须是技术权威”的执念。你的工作是引导、赋能、掌舵，而不是事事亲力亲为。带工程师不是一次升职；它是一份全新的工作。

Engineering Leadership Is About Being a “Generalist with Range”

工程领导力，是做一个“有广度的通才”

You’ve probably heard the phrase “jack of all trades, master of none,” and maybe even felt a little queasy about it. But that’s precisely what you need to be in an engineering leadership role. You don’t need to be the world’s best coder, nor do you need to be a product strategy expert. What you need is to have a little bit of knowledge about many things and the ability to move between them effortlessly.

你大概听过那句话：“门门通，门门松”（jack of all trades, master of none），甚至可能对此有点反感。但在工程领导岗上，你恰恰需要成为这样的人。你不需要是全世界最牛的程序员，也不需要是产品战略专家。你需要的是：对很多事情都略知一二，并且能在它们之间自如切换。

In his 1973 novel Time Enough for Love, Robert A. Heinlein said, “Specialization is for insects.” And it’s true, while engineers are often specialists, leaders must be generalists. You need to be able to step into different domains—strategy, people management, and product alignment—without getting bogged down in technical details.

Robert A. Heinlein 在他 1973 年的小说《时间足够你爱》（Time Enough for Love）里说过：“专业化是虫子干的事。”这话不假——工程师往往是专才，而领导者必须是通才。你需要能踏入不同领域——战略、人员管理、产品对齐——而不被技术细节缠住手脚。

But let’s be clear: this isn’t an excuse for shallow thinking. Being a generalist means you have a broad understanding of how everything fits together and the insight to know when to go deep. It’s about context switching with purpose, not just skimming the surface.

但要说清楚：这绝不是浅尝辄止的借口。做通才意味着你对“万事万物如何相互咬合”有广博的理解，并有判断何时该下钻深度的洞察力。它是有目的的上下文切换，而不是浮在表面上浅浅掠过。

— 原书第 36 页 —

Action Beats Inaction Every Time

行动永远胜过不行动

In a chaotic environment, the risk isn’t that you’ll do the wrong thing; it’s that you’ll do nothing at all. There’s a tendency to freeze up when you don’t have all the answers, waiting for clarity that may never come. But here’s the truth: taking action is (almost always) better than standing still.

在混乱的环境里，风险不在于你做错事，而在于你什么都不做。当你没有全部答案时，人很容易僵在原地，等待那份也许永远不会到来的清晰。但真相是：采取行动（几乎总是）胜过原地不动。

One of the most powerful traits of a great leader is a bias toward action. Even if you’re unsure about the outcome, moving forward is better than waiting around. In chaotic environments, decisions are often made with incomplete information, and that’s okay. It’s better to make a decision, adapt, and iterate than to remain stuck.

伟大领导者最强大的特质之一，就是“偏向行动”。即便你对结果没有把握，向前走也比原地等待强。在混乱环境里，决策往往是在信息不完整的情况下做出的，这没什么大不了。做个决定、然后调整、迭代，远比困在原地要好。

And here’s the good news we talked about in Chapter 1: chaos creates opportunity. Taking action, especially when no one else is willing to, sets you apart and builds momentum for your team. Don’t be afraid to seek out opportunities to lead, even when the path isn’t clear.

还记得我们在第 1 章说过的好消息吗：混乱孕育机遇。采取行动——尤其是在没人愿意站出来的时候——会让你脱颖而出，并为团队积累势头。不要害怕主动寻找领导的机会，哪怕道路还不清晰。

Role Description: A Do-It-Yourself Blueprint

角色说明书：一份自己动手画的蓝图

So, how do you make sense of it all? How do you take control of the chaos and define your role in a way that brings clarity, focus, and direction to your team? It all starts with documenting your responsibilities. This is one of the first “hard parts” of your new role: communicating (in this case, writing well).

那么，你怎么把这一切理顺？你怎么掌控混乱、定义自己的角色，从而为团队带来清晰、专注和方向？一切都始于把你的职责写下来。这是你新岗位上最先遇到的“难啃的骨头”之一：沟通能力（这里具体指——写得清楚）。

In the following sections, we’ll break down the five foundational pillars: people, mission, plan, process, and product. As you work through each section, you’ll have the opportunity to reflect on your current situation and define specific responsibilities that map to your unique challenges. By the end of this chapter, you’ll have a clear, personalized role description that guides your leadership and helps you stay grounded, even when everything else is shifting around you.

在接下来的几节里，我们会逐一拆解五大根基支柱：人、使命、计划、流程、产品。每过一节，你都有机会反思自己当下的处境，并定义出对应你独特挑战的具体职责。读完本章，你会拥有一份清晰的、为你量身定制的角色说明书——它将指引你的领导工作，帮你在周围一切都在变动时仍能站稳脚跟。

Rather than being static, this blueprint is a living document that you’ll refine and adapt as you grow. Whether you’re building a team from scratch, inheriting a fractured group of engineers, or guiding a well-established team through turbulent times, this framework will give you the structure and clarity you need to lead effectively.

这份蓝图不是静态的，而是一份“活的文件”，会随着你的成长不断打磨、调整。无论你是从零搭团队、接手一个四分五裂的工程师小组，还是带领一支成熟团队穿越动荡时期，这个框架都能给你有效领导所需的结构与清晰。

The first pillar is people. Before you can deliver a product, ship features, or implement processes, you need to understand the team that will build it all. Leadership starts with the people in front of you.

第一根支柱是人。在你交付产品、上线功能、落地流程之前，你需要先了解那个将要把这一切建起来的团队。领导力，从你眼前的这些人开始。

— 原书第 37 页 —

It’s a common thought: “I’ve already got a job description and a team charter. Why do I need to define my role again?” Well, let’s be real; most job descriptions are just glorified ads—aspirational and often out of touch with the reality of your day-to-day work. They’re usually written before you even step into the role, and while they might look nice on paper, they rarely survive first contact with the actual job.

你可能会想：“我已经有岗位说明书和团队章程了，为什么还要重新定义自己的角色？” 说实话，大多数岗位说明书不过是美化过的招聘广告——写的都是理想状态，往往和你日常工作的现实脱节。它们通常在你入职之前就写好了，纸面光鲜，但很少能在你真正上手工作后还站得住脚。

And charters? They often suffer the same fate—vague, filled with boilerplate language, or created in some long-forgotten workshop and never updated. Roles evolve, responsibilities shift, and those documents rarely reflect the new challenges you’re taking on.

至于团队章程呢？下场往往也差不多——含糊不清、套话连篇，或者是在某个早就被遗忘的研讨会上写出来后就再没更新过。角色在演进，职责在变化，而那些文件很少能反映你正在面对的新挑战。

The real question is: does your job description reflect what you actually do? If not, having something more grounded can be a game changer. It gives you a clearer sense of direction and a tool to help you track your progress when it’s time to showcase what you’ve been accomplishing.

真正的问题是：你的岗位说明书反映的是你实际在做的事吗？如果不是，拥有一份更接地气的文件可能会成为转折点。它会给你更清晰的方向感，也会在你需要展示自己成果时，成为帮你追踪进展的工具。

People: It All Starts with Your Team

人：一切都从你的团队开始

You’ve got the title, the responsibilities, and the office (maybe). But leadership? That starts with your people. No team means no leadership. It’s not about getting them to do the work; it’s about building something more significant than any individual effort. Your job is to ensure that your team isn’t just a collection of talented engineers but a crew creating something extraordinary together.

你有了头衔、有了职责、也有了办公室（也许吧）。但领导力呢？它从你的人开始。没有团队，就无所谓领导。这不是让他们去干活，而是要构建一件比任何个人努力都更伟大的事情。你的工作是确保你的团队不只是一群有才华的工程师的集合，而是一支共同创造非凡事物的队伍。

But where do you start? Maybe you’ve inherited a team with a history you didn’t write, or you’re in the enviable position of building one from scratch. In either case, leadership starts with listening and seeing clearly. Don’t get lost in the noise of missed deadlines, feature churn, or tech debt. The first task is always understanding your people—what makes them tick, what holds them back, and how you can help them grow into something stronger.

但你从哪里入手？也许你接手了一支历史你并未参与书写的团队，又或许你处于令人羡慕的位置——从零开始搭一支。无论哪种情况，领导力都从倾听和看清现状开始。不要迷失在错过的截止日期、功能反复改动、技术债的喧嚣里。第一件事永远是了解你的人：是什么让他们有动力、是什么在拖他们的后腿、你如何帮助他们成长为更强大的人。

What’s Your Starting Point?

你的起点在哪里？

Every team comes with a backstory, and before you start leading, you need to figure out which chapter you’re in. Are you stepping into a well-oiled machine or taking charge of a team struggling with miscommunication and missed opportunities? Maybe they’ve been worn down by constant pivots, or perhaps they’re a group of rockstars who only play solos, and don’t collaborate. Wherever they are, your first move is to understand the dynamics already at work.

Mission: You’ve Got a Crew; Now You Need a Place to Go

使命：你有了一支队伍，现在还得有个要去的地方

You’ve got your team assembled. They’re working, shipping code, and pushing through “sprints.” But the question is, do they know why? What are they working toward? And more importantly, do they care?

你的团队已经凑齐了。他们在干活、在交付代码、在一个个“冲刺”里硬推。但问题是：他们知道为什么吗？他们在朝什么努力？更重要的是——他们在乎吗？

Your job isn’t just to manage projects or move features across a Kanban board; it’s to connect your team to a mission bigger than themselves. Engineers thrive when they understand what they’re building and why it matters. They need to see the bigger picture: how their work shapes the product, impacts users, and drives the company forward. Without that connection, even the most talented team will drift. We, as leaders, solve problems. So, the goal is to get your team closer to the problems!

你的工作不只是管项目、把功能在看板上拖来拖去；而是把团队和一个比他们自身更大的使命连接起来。当工程师理解自己在造什么、以及为什么重要时，他们才会蓬勃生长。他们需要看到全局：自己的工作如何塑造产品、影响用户、推动公司向前。没有这种连接，再聪明的团队也会漂移。我们作为领导者是来解决问题的，所以目标就是让你的团队离问题更近！

The mission might not always be perfectly defined by leadership, but that doesn’t mean your team can’t have its own mission. Where to Start

从哪里入手

If your team isn’t already connected to the company’s mission, that’s your starting point. But don’t expect a corporate vision statement alone to inspire them. Your job is to turn that high-level mission into something tangible. Engineers need to understand how their work contributes—whether by improving the user experience, driving product adoption, or supporting key business goals. It’s not enough for them to know the mission exists; they need to see how their daily efforts make a measurable impact.

如果你的团队还没和公司使命连起来，那就是你的起点。但别指望一句公司愿景口号就能激励他们。你的工作是把那个高层使命变成看得见摸得着的东西。工程师需要理解自己的工作如何做贡献——无论是改善用户体验、推动产品采用，还是支撑关键业务目标。光让他们知道“使命存在”是不够的；他们需要看到自己每天的努力如何产生可衡量的影响。

If the company’s mission is unclear or changes frequently, you need to step in and create clarity for your team by translating the company’s priorities into something your team can act on. Whatever the goal, ensure your team has a clear, actionable direction that aligns with the company’s broader objectives, even if those objectives feel a bit uncertain.

如果公司的使命不清晰或者频繁变动，你就要介入，把公司的优先级翻译成团队能执行的东西，为他们创造清晰。这个目标可能是为产品建立稳定性，也可能是减少用户的摩擦。无论目标是什么，确保你的团队有一个清晰、可执行的方向——它与公司更宏大的目标对齐，哪怕那些目标本身感觉还有点不确定。

Getting Your Team on Board

让团队真正认同

Once you’ve clarified the mission, the next challenge is getting your team to care about it. It’s easy to assume that engineers are aligned just because they’re doing the work, but real alignment goes beyond completing tasks; it requires personal connection.

一旦你把使命厘清，下一个挑战就是让团队真正在乎它。人很容易以为：工程师既然在干活，那就是对齐了。但真正的对齐远不止完成任务；它需要个人层面的连接。

Your team needs to feel that they’re not only delivering features but solving meaningful problems. And that sense of purpose doesn’t come from the top down alone; it comes from you, bridging the gap between technical work and real-world impact. Help them see how that new API they’re building will improve the customer experience, or how an infrastructure upgrade is laying the groundwork for future scalability.

你的团队需要感受到：他们不只是在交付功能，而是在解决有意义的问题。而这种目标感不是单靠自上而下传递的；它来自于你——你在技术工作和现实世界影响之间架起桥梁。帮他们看到：他们正在写的那个新 API 将如何改善客户体验；一次基础设施升级又如何为未来的可扩展性打下地基。

The key is to show them that their work has tangible value. When engineers understand that what they’re building is a solution to a real problem, they become more motivated, creative, and invested. They stop thinking of themselves as just executors of tasks and start seeing themselves as contributors to something larger. And that’s when the magic happens—because a motivated, mission-driven team often exceeds expectations.

关键是让他们看到自己的工作有实实在在的价值。当工程师理解自己造的东西是在解决一个真实问题时，他们会变得更有动力、更有创造力、更投入。他们不再把自己仅仅看作任务的执行者，而开始把自己看作某个更大事物的贡献者。而奇迹往往就在这时发生——因为一支被激励、被使命驱动的团队，常常会超出预期。

Turn the Mission into Action

把使命变成行动

So, you’ve got the mission. But how do you make it real? A vision is useless without action, and your team needs more than high-level goals; they need concrete, measurable objectives that make the mission tangible in their day-to-day work.

好，你有了使命。但你怎么让它落地？没有行动的愿景毫无用处。你的团队需要的不只是高层目标；他们需要具体的、可衡量的目标，让使命在日常工作中变得可触可感。

If you’re responsible for setting goals, ensure they align with the company’s mission and are specific enough to drive action. For example, rather than just aiming to “improve performance,” tie it to something meaningful: “Reduce customer onboarding time by 20%.” Instead of focusing on “reducing technical debt,” consider linking it to “increasing uptime to support enterprise clients.” This is how you turn the mission into something your engineers can sink their teeth into. When they see how their work makes an impact, they’ll be more engaged, focused, and driven to push the boundaries of what’s possible.

如果你负责定目标，确保它们与公司使命对齐、并且具体到足以驱动行动。例如，不要只说“提升性能”，而要把它绑到有意义的东西上：“把客户上手时间缩短 20%”。不要只盯着“减少技术债”，而要把它和“提高可用率以支持企业客户”挂钩。这就是把使命变成工程师能咬得动的东西的方法。当他们看到自己的工作如何产生影响，他们会更投入、更专注、更有动力去突破可能性的边界。

And if your company’s mission is unclear, don’t wait around for direction; go get it. Connect with the product, marketing, and leadership teams. Understand the broader business goals and bring that clarity back to your team. Beyond just managing code delivery, your job is to create a bridge between business objectives and technical execution. In doing so, you will be ensuring that your team’s work is aligned with the company’s strategy, even when the roadmap is constantly evolving.

如果公司的使命不清晰，不要干等着方向掉下来；主动去把它找回来。去和产品、市场、领导团队聊。理解更宏观的业务目标，然后把那份清晰带回给你的团队。除了管理代码交付之外，你的工作是在业务目标和技术执行之间架起一座桥。这样做，你就能确保团队的工作与公司战略对齐——哪怕路线图一直在变。

Exercise: Mission Alignment with Measurable Impact

练习：使命对齐与可衡量的影响

This exercise will help you to define concrete, measurable approaches to connecting your team with the company’s mission. Instead of vague alignment goals, you’ll create specific indicators that show whether your team is genuinely connected to meaningful work.

这个练习会帮你定义具体、可衡量的方法，把团队和公司使命连接起来。不要含糊的对齐目标，你要创造具体的指标，来判断团队是否真的与有意义的工作相连。

Step 1: Diagnose Current Disconnection

第 1 步：诊断当前的脱节

Pick one symptom from Chapter 1 that your team is experiencing. Then identify how disconnection with the company’s mission might be contributing to it. Example answer:

Our team has high levels of context switching and unclear priorities. I think this happens because we take on any urgent request without understanding what projects actually matter most to the company’s success.

我们团队上下文切换严重、优先级不清。我认为原因是：我们接下任何紧急请求，却没搞清楚哪些项目对公司成功真正最重要。

What would change if your team truly understood how their work connects to company success? Write one specific, measurable change you’d expect to see in 90 days. Example answer:

如果你的团队真正理解了自己的工作如何与公司成功相连，会有什么改变？写下一个具体、可衡量的变化——你期望在 90 天内看到它发生。示例回答：

Engineers are able to explain in their own words how their current project connects to company goals, and we spend less than 20% of our capacity on unplanned work that doesn’t align with strategic objectives.

工程师能用自己的话解释当前项目如何与公司目标相连；我们用于与战略目标不对齐的非计划工作的精力低于 20%。

第 3 步：制定行动计划

List two to three concrete actions that you’ll take to achieve this outcome. Make them specific enough that someone else could execute them. Example answer:

列出两到三个为达成这个结果你会采取的具体行动。要具体到别人也能照着执行。示例回答：

  • Hold monthly impact sessions where we trace infrastructure improvements to customer outcomes (faster deploys lead to quicker feature delivery, which lead to faster user feedback loops).

    每月举办一次影响复盘会，把基础设施改进追溯到客户结果（更快的部署带来更快的功能交付，进而带来更快的用户反馈闭环）。

    每季度与业务领导一起做路线图复盘，确保平台优先级与公司战略对齐。

    跟踪并分享指标，展示平台改进如何赋能功能团队的交付速度。

第 4 步：选一个先行指标

How will you know within 30 days whether this approach is working? Choose something you can measure quickly. Example answer:

你怎么在 30 天内判断这个方法是否奏效？选一个你能快速衡量的东西。示例回答：

In team meetings, engineers start connecting their work to business outcomes without prompting, and feature team requests include business justification rather than just urgency claims.

在团队会议上，工程师会在没有人提示的情况下主动把自己的工作和业务结果连起来；功能团队提需求时会附上业务理由，而不只是喊“紧急”。

The goal is to connect daily work to meaningful outcomes in ways you can actually measure, rather than just hoping for cultural change that might never materialize.

目标是用你真正能衡量的方式，把日常工作和有意义的结果连接起来——而不是空想一场也许永远不会发生的文化变革。

Plan: You Know Where to Go; Now Chart the Course

计划：你知道要去哪了，现在把航线画出来

It’s one thing to know where you’re headed, but it’s another thing entirely to map out how to get there. While a mission gives your team a destination, what about the plan? Without a roadmap, even the most talented engineers can get lost. A plan should do more than just list tasks; it must create focus, alignment, and momentum.

知道要去哪是一回事，把怎么去画出来是完全另一回事。使命给了团队目的地，那计划呢？没有路线图，再聪明的工程师也会迷路。计划不应该只是罗列任务；它必须创造专注、对齐和势头。

But here’s the twist: you’re not expected to create the plan alone. The best plans are built collaboratively, bringing in insights from all directions. That means liaising with your cross-functional partners in product, design, and marketing teams, and empowering your technical leads to take ownership of parts of the roadmap. A leader who plans alone is destined for bottlenecks, but a leader who plans with others sets the stage for execution at scale.

但这里有个转折：没人指望你一个人把计划做出来。最好的计划是协作出来的，汇集各方洞见。这意味着你要和产品、设计、市场的跨职能伙伴对接，并授权你的技术负责人拥有路线图的一部分。一个人闷头做计划的领导者，注定会遇到瓶颈；而和大家一起做计划的领导者，则为大规模执行搭好了舞台。

Build with Your Partners

和你的伙伴一起构建

If you think you can map out the perfect plan on your own, you’re probably setting yourself up for failure. As a leader, your job isn’t to have all the answers; it’s to ask the right questions and bring in the right people. Rather than being created in isolation, great plans result from collaboration across functions, with product managers who understand customer needs, marketing teams that see market shifts, and sales teams who comprehend customer pain points.

如果你觉得自己一个人就能画出完美计划，那你大概是在自找失败。作为领导者，你的工作不是掌握所有答案；而是提出对的问题、把对的人拉进来。好的计划不是闭门造车做出来的，而是跨职能协作的结果——产品经理懂客户需求，市场团队看得到市场动向，销售团队理解客户痛点。

Aligning engineering’s efforts with the company’s broader goals requires an in-depth understanding of business priorities, product vision, and customer impact. So start by building strong relationships with your partners in those departments. Sit down with the product team to understand what’s coming down the pipeline, and connect with sales to learn what’s breaking the deal. The more context you have, the better you can translate business needs into engineering goals.

要让工程的努力与公司更宏大的目标对齐，需要你深入理解业务优先级、产品愿景和客户影响。所以，先和这些部门的伙伴建立牢固关系。坐下来和产品团队聊聊，看管道里接下来是什么；和销售聊聊，听听是什么在卡住成单。你掌握的上下文越多，就越能把业务需求翻译成工程目标。

And don’t forget about your technical leads. The engineers closest to the code often have the best sense of where things could go wrong or where potential opportunities lie. Bring them into the planning process and let them own pieces of the roadmap, so that they become leaders in driving the plan forward.

也别忘了你的技术负责人。离代码最近的工程师，往往最清楚哪里可能出问题、哪里可能有机会。把他们拉进计划过程，让他们拥有路线图的一部分，这样他们就会成为推动计划前进的领导者。

Know What to Prioritize

知道该优先做什么

A plan is only useful if it helps your team focus on what matters most. When everything is important, nothing is. This is where the magic of prioritization comes

一个计划只有在能帮团队聚焦最重要的事时才有用。当一切都重要时，就等于什么都不重要。优先级排序的魔力就在这里

— 原书第 45 页 —

in. The challenge isn’t figuring out what your team can do; it’s deciding what they should do right now to deliver the most value. And remember: it’s not prioritizing if it doesn’t hurt. If you’re not making tough calls, you’re not really prioritizing.

发挥作用。挑战不在于搞清楚团队能做什么，而在于决定他们现在该做什么才能交付最大价值。记住：如果一件事不“疼”，那就不叫优先级。如果你没在做艰难的抉择，你就不是在真正地排优先级。

So ask yourself: what’s going to move the needle the fastest? Should you focus on shipping features that drive growth, or is your tech debt piling up to the point where it’s slowing everything down? Is your infrastructure holding back scalability, or is there a feature that could unlock new customer adoption? The answer won’t always be obvious, and it won’t always stay the same. But as a leader, you need to be decisive.

所以问问自己：什么事能最快推动指针？你该聚焦在驱动增长的功能上，还是技术债已经堆到拖慢一切的地步？你的基础设施是在拖可扩展性的后腿，还是有个功能能打开新的客户采用？答案不会总是显而易见，也不会一成不变。但作为领导者，你必须果断。

In prioritization, sometimes, saying no is more important than saying yes. Roadmaps and backlogs are filled with good ideas, but you should only pursue the most relevant and important ones. Saying “not today” is usually challenging, but remember that a “no” today is not “never”; it’s just not today. Your team needs clarity, which means making those tough decisions. When you clearly communicate the reasons behind those decisions, your engineers will be confident to move forward without second-guessing. They’ll understand not just what they’re doing but why they’re doing it.

在排优先级时，有时候说“不”比说“好”更重要。路线图和待办列表里塞满了好点子，但你只应该去追那些最相关、最重要的。说“今天先不做”通常不容易，但请记住：今天的“不”不是“永远不”，只是“今天先不”。你的团队需要清晰，这意味着你要做出那些艰难的决定。当你把这些决定背后的理由讲清楚，你的工程师就能自信地向前走、不再反复猜忌。他们不仅会理解自己在做什么，还会理解为什么要做。

Turn Strategy into Action

把战略变成行动

A plan is worthless if it doesn’t get executed. To move from strategy to action, break down high-level goals into actionable steps that your team can rally around. It’s not enough to say, “We need to improve performance.” What does that look like in practice? Does it mean upgrading the architecture, refactoring old code, or optimizing the database? Every big goal needs to be distilled into specific, measurable objectives.

一个计划如果不被执行，就一文不值。要从战略走到行动，把高层目标拆解成团队能凝聚起来去做的可执行步骤。光说“我们需要提升性能”是不够的。那在实践中到底长什么样？是升级架构、重构老代码，还是优化数据库？每个大目标都需要被提炼成具体、可衡量的子目标。

It’s important to delegate responsibilities, rather than attempting to execute alone. Trust your technical leads to take ownership of key parts of the plan. Instead of micromanaging, your job is to steer the ship. Trust your leads to handle the details while you keep an eye on the horizon, ensuring the team stays aligned with the bigger picture.

重要的是要把职责授权下去，而不是试图一个人执行。信任你的技术负责人，让他们拥有计划的关键部分。你的工作不是微观管理，而是掌舵。信任你的负责人去处理细节，而你自己盯着地平线，确保团队不偏离大局。

It’s also important to build checkpoints into your plan. Don’t wait until the project’s done to see if things are on track. Set milestones along the way—clear markers that enable you to assess progress and course correct if needed. These checkpoints guide your team, letting them adjust without losing sight of the end goal.

在计划里设置检查点也很重要。不要等到项目做完了才看事情是否在轨道上。沿途设置里程碑——清晰的标记，让你能评估进展、必要时纠偏。这些检查点指引你的团队，让他们在调整时不会丢掉最终目标。

Adjust, but Stay Focused

调整，但保持专注

No plan survives first contact with reality. Things will change; priorities will shift, new information will come to light, and unexpected obstacles will arise. Great leaders know how to stay flexible without losing focus. When the roadmap changes, it’s your job to keep the team grounded. The core objectives don’t change, even when the tactics do.

没有任何计划能在与现实第一次交锋后还完好无损。事情会变；优先级会转移，新信息会浮出水面，意外的障碍会冒出来。伟大的领导者知道如何在保持灵活的同时不丢掉专注。路线图变了，你的工作是让团队稳住。核心目标不变——哪怕战术变了。

— 原书第 46 页 —

This doesn’t mean constantly reworking the plan, but rather staying nimble and reevaluating when necessary. Maybe a new opportunity has opened up that’s too good to pass up, or maybe product feedback has shifted a feature’s priority. When things change, don’t panic—adapt. But always ensure your team understands how these changes fit into the broader mission. They must feel like they’re still moving forward, even when the path shifts.

这并不意味着不停地返工改计划，而是保持敏捷、在必要时重新评估。也许出现了一个好到不能错过的新机会，也许产品反馈改变了某个功能的优先级。事情变了，别慌——去适应。但一定要确保团队理解这些变化如何嵌入更宏大的使命。他们必须感到：哪怕路径变了，自己仍在向前走。

Exercise: Defining Your Role in Strategic Planning

练习：定义你在战略规划中的角色

既然你已经探索了如何制定一个能驱动专注与对齐的计划，现在是时候把它转化为你领导角色中可执行的职责了。这个练习会帮你定义如何协作、如何排优先级、以及如何确保团队走在轨道上。

Step 1: Assess Your Current Planning Approach

做完这个练习，你就定义了该如何做规划——从协作到排优先级，再到把战略变成可执行步骤。一个清晰、经过深思熟虑的计划是执行的脊梁，确保团队知道要去哪、以及怎么去。

Process: The System That Keeps Things Moving

流程：让事情持续运转的系统

You can have the best team, the clearest mission, and the smartest plan, but if your processes are a mess, then none of it matters. Process is the engine that powers execution. Done right, it keeps your team efficient, focused, and productive. Done wrong, and it becomes the bottleneck that grinds everything to a halt.

你可以有最棒的团队、最清晰的使命、最聪明的计划，但如果流程一团糟，那一切都白搭。流程是驱动执行的引擎。做对了，它让团队高效、专注、高产；做错了，它就变成把一切都磨停的瓶颈。

So, what is the key to great process? Less is more. You don’t need to create an elaborate system of approvals and checkpoints, as this leads to bureaucracy. Instead, what you need is a framework that enables work to flow smoothly without getting in the way. The best ones are there to support, not to control.

那么，好流程的关键是什么？少即是多。你不需要搭一套繁复的审批和检查点系统——那只会导致官僚主义。你需要的是一个让工作顺畅流动、而不是挡在路中间的框架。最好的流程是来托举的，不是来控制的。

Keep It Lean, but Effective

保持精简，但要有效

When it comes to processes, complexity is the enemy. If your team is bogged down by long approval cycles, endless meetings, or cumbersome code reviews, they’ll lose momentum and motivation. Great processes are lightweight and designed to remove friction rather than add it.

谈到流程，复杂就是敌人。如果你的团队被漫长的审批周期、没完没了的会议、或笨重的代码评审拖住，他们会失去势头和动力。好的流程是轻量的，设计初衷是消除摩擦，而不是增加摩擦。

But simplicity doesn’t mean a free-for-all. You still need structure, code reviews, deployment processes, and feedback loops, but these should be streamlined to keep things moving. If a process is dragging, take a step back and ask, “Is this helping us get better, or is it slowing us down?” If it’s the latter, cut it.

但简单不等于放任自流。你仍然需要结构、代码评审、部署流程和反馈循环，但这些都应该被精简到能让事情持续流动。如果某个流程在拖后腿，退一步问问：“这是在帮我们变好，还是在拖慢我们？” 如果是后者，砍掉它。

— 原书第 48 页 —

Make Process a Team Effort

让流程成为团队共同的事

You’re not the only one responsible for defining the process. The best processes are created with or by the team, not for the team. Your engineers are the ones who have to live with these processes every day, so it only makes sense to involve them in shaping how things are done.

定义流程不是你一个人的责任。最好的流程是和团队一起、或者由团队自己创造的，而不是为团队强加的。你的工程师是每天都要在这些流程里生活的人，所以让他们参与塑造做事方式才合理。

This isn’t just about efficiency but about ownership. When your team has a hand in creating the process, they’re far more likely to follow through and keep things running smoothly. Create space for feedback and be open to adjustments when things aren’t working. Process is a living system, not a static rulebook.

这不只是为了效率，更是为了主人翁意识。当团队参与了流程的创建，他们更可能真正遵守它、让事情顺畅运转。为反馈留出空间，当事情不对时乐于调整。流程是一个活的系统，不是一本静态的规则手册。

Adjust As You Go

边走边调

No process is perfect forever. What worked when your team consisted of 5 people might fall apart now that you’re a team of 20. Processes need to evolve as your team grows and the complexity of your work increases. That means regularly evaluating how things are going—considering what’s working, what’s slowing the team down, and where improvements can be made.

没有哪个流程能永远完美。团队 5 个人时管用的做法，到了 20 个人时可能就崩了。流程需要随着团队成长和工作复杂度提升而演进。这意味着要定期评估进展——看看什么在奏效、什么在拖团队后腿、哪里可以改进。

Don’t be afraid to change what’s not working. Just because a process was useful last quarter doesn’t mean it’s relevant now. Keep things flexible, and don’t hesitate to scrap something if it’s no longer serving the team.

不要害怕改掉不管用的东西。一个流程上个季度还有用，不代表现在还有意义。保持灵活，如果某件事不再服务于团队，不要犹豫，直接扔掉。

Exercise: The Process Pulse Survey

练习：流程脉搏调研

Most leaders guess at process problems instead of measuring them. Your team knows exactly where the friction is; you just need to ask the right questions. In the end, they are the ones who consume your “process.” Listen to your users.

大多数领导者对流程问题靠猜，而不是去衡量。你的团队确切地知道摩擦在哪里；你只是需要问对问题。说到底，他们才是“消费”你流程的人。听你的用户怎么说。

Deploy this two-minute anonymous survey to track team productivity patterns:

发下面这份两分钟匿名调研，来追踪团队的生产力模式：

  1. This week, how often did you get to work uninterrupted for 2+ hours?

    这周你有多少次能不受打扰地连续工作 2 小时以上？

    • a. Most days

      a. 几乎每天

    • b. A few times

      b. 几次

    • c. Once or twice

      c. 一两次

    • d. Not at all

      d. 完全没有

  2. How often do you find unofficial ways to get things done?

    你有多频繁地会找“非正式”途径把事办完？

    • a. Never—official processes work fine.

      a. 从不——正式流程挺顺的。

    • b. Occasionally—for edge cases.

      b. 偶尔——用于边缘情况。

    • c. Regularly—it’s faster.

      c. 经常——那样更快。

    • d. Always—it’s the only way.

      d. 总是——那是唯一的办法。

    3. — 原书第 49 页 —

  3. What do you spend the most time waiting for?

    你花最多时间在等什么？

    • a. Reviews or approvals

      a. 评审或审批

    • b. Other people’s work

      b. 别人的工作

    • c. Access or permissions

      c. 访问权限或许可

    • d. Decisions from above

      d. 上面的决策

    • e. Information or clarification

      e. 信息或澄清

    • f. Nothing significant

      f. 没什么特别的

  4. For the work you do daily, how quickly can you usually get the go-ahead?

    对于你日常做的工作，你通常多快能拿到许可？

    • a. Immediately

      a. 立刻

    • b. Same day

      b. 当天

    • c. One or two days

      c. 一两天

    • d. A week or more

      d. 一周或更久

  5. What would you tell a new teammate if they asked, “How do things really work around here?”

    如果有新同事问你：“这地方实际是怎么运转的？”你会怎么说？

  6. Complete this sentence: “If I could change one thing about how we work, I would…”

    把这句话补完：“如果我能改变我们工作方式中的一件事，我会……”

Reading the Results

解读结果

Start by listening, not reacting. The “process pulse” survey reveals how work actually flows, not how you think it does. Look for patterns. Are people waiting on approvals, inventing workarounds, or struggling to find focus time? These are signals of friction, not complaints. The open-ended responses often reveal the real story, including the unspoken rules, backdoor processes, and quiet trade-offs that shape your culture. Together, they show how work truly gets done.

先倾听，别急着反应。“流程脉搏”调研揭示的是工作实际如何流动，而不是你以为它如何流动。寻找模式：人们在等审批吗？在发明绕行方案吗？还是在挣扎着找专注时间？这些是摩擦的信号，不是抱怨。开放题的回答往往揭示真正的故事——包括那些不成文的规则、后门流程、以及塑造你文化的安静取舍。它们合在一起，展示工作到底是怎么完成的。

Iterating Toward Fixes

迭代走向修复

Be thoughtful about how you try to address the issues. Most leaders try to fix everything at once, and nothing changes. Instead, focus on one thing. Find the single pattern that slows down the most people the most often, and design a two-week experiment to improve it.

考虑如何解决这些问题时要审慎。大多数领导者想一次把所有问题都修了，结果什么都没变。相反，聚焦在一件事上。找到那个最频繁地拖慢最多人的单一模式，设计一个两周实验来改善它。

Keep it small and fast. The goal is progress, not perfection. Here are some possible experiments:

保持小而快。目标是进步，不是完美。下面是一些可能的实验：

  • Approve routine changes the same day.

    当天审批例行变更。

  • Protect two-hour focus blocks each morning.

    每天上午保护两小时的专注时段。

  • Create a fast lane for small, low-risk requests.

    为小的、低风险的请求开辟快车道。

  • Simplify deployment steps to remove waiting.

    简化部署步骤以消除等待。

— 原书第 50 页 —

These small shifts send a signal: improvement is possible, feedback matters, and bureaucracy is not the default.

这些小小的改变会发出一个信号：改进是可能的、反馈是被重视的、官僚主义不是默认状态。

Measuring Impact

衡量影响

Rerun the pulse after two weeks. Look for changes in both metrics and mood: more flow time, fewer workarounds, faster decisions, and a working environment that feels lighter.

两周后重新做一次脉搏调研。在指标和氛围两个方面寻找变化：更多的流畅时间、更少的绕行方案、更快的决策、以及一个感觉更轻松的工作环境。

Share what you learn. Celebrate progress, acknowledge what did not work, and keep the loop going. Trust grows when teams see their feedback turn into action, and over time, that trust becomes the engine of continuous improvement.

分享你学到的东西。庆祝进展，承认哪些没奏效，让这个循环转下去。当团队看到自己的反馈变成了行动，信任就会增长；而随着时间推移，这份信任会成为持续改进的引擎。

We’ll talk more about processes and collaboration in Chapters 6 and 9.

关于流程和协作，我们会在第 6 章和第 9 章进一步讨论。

Product: What Are We Actually Delivering?

产品：我们到底在交付什么？

At the end of the day, it’s all about results. Your team might be pushing code, but are they delivering outcomes that drive the business forward? In engineering, it’s easy to get caught up in shipping features, closing tickets, and hitting deadlines. But all that means nothing if what you’re delivering doesn’t solve real problems or create user value. Outcomes matter more than output.

说到底，一切都关乎结果。你的团队也许在使劲推代码，但他们交付的结果真的在推动业务前进吗？在工程领域，人很容易陷入交付功能、关 ticket、赶截止日期的忙碌里。但如果你交付的东西不解决真实问题、不创造用户价值，那这一切都毫无意义。结果（outcome）比产出（output）更重要。

This is where leadership steps in. Your job is to make sure the work your team is doing translates into real-world impact. Whether that’s a customer-facing feature, a critical infrastructure upgrade, or an internal tool that boosts productivity, your team’s work needs to move the needle. The best leaders don’t just focus on getting things done; they focus on getting the right things done. And that’s the difference between a team that just releases features and a team that delivers value.

这正是领导力该上场的地方。你的工作是确保团队做的事能转化为现实世界的影响。无论是面向客户的功能、关键的基础设施升级，还是一个提升生产力的内部工具，团队的工作都需要真正推动指针。最好的领导者不只关注把事做完；他们关注把对的事做完。这就是“只会发功能的团队”和“能交付价值的团队”之间的区别。

Know What Success Looks Like

知道成功长什么样

Your team will chase the wrong goals if you don’t define success. And hitting a deadline or closing a sprint doesn’t always mean success. The real question is: what problem are you solving? Are you building something that genuinely makes a difference to your users or the business, or are you just shipping for the sake of shipping?

如果你不定义成功，团队就会去追错的目标。而赶上截止日期、关完一个冲刺，并不总意味着成功。真正的问题是：你在解决什么问题？你在造的东西是真的给用户或业务带来了改变，还是仅仅为了发而发？

It’s your job to guide your engineers toward the impact of their work, not just the output. Every feature and every line of code should be tied to a clear outcome. Are you improving user experience? Are you making the product faster, more reliable, or easier to use? Are you enabling the company to scale, grow revenue, or reduce costs? When your team can see the impact of what they’re building, they’ll care more, innovate faster, and take pride in their work.

你的工作是引导工程师去关注工作的影响，而不只是产出。每个功能、每一行代码都应该绑在一个清晰的结果上。你是在改善用户体验吗？是在让产品更快、更可靠、还是更好用？是在让公司能扩张、增长收入，还是降低成本？当你的团队能看到自己所造之物的影响，他们会更在乎、更快创新、并为自己的工作感到自豪。

— 原书第 51 页 —

In reality, success is fluid. It might be releasing a new feature this quarter, and it could be driving down infrastructure costs next quarter. Success is about delivering value, and values change as the business evolves. Your role is to keep that focus clear, even as priorities shift.

现实里，成功是流动的。这个季度可能是发布一个新功能，下个季度可能是把基础设施成本打下来。成功在于交付价值，而价值会随着业务演进而变化。你的角色是：哪怕优先级在变，也要让团队的焦点保持清晰。

Balance Quality with Speed

在质量与速度之间取得平衡

Speed is critical. Shipping fast gets you ahead of the competition, unlocks new opportunities, and helps the company grow. But speed without quality? That’s a disaster waiting to happen. Too often, teams push to ship faster, only to cut corners, leading to tech debt, bugs, and dissatisfied users. Shipping fast isn’t enough; you need to ship well.

速度至关重要。快速交付让你跑在竞争前面、打开新机会、帮助公司成长。但没有质量的速度呢？那是一场等待发生的灾难。太多时候，团队为了发得更快而抄近道，结果带来技术债、bug 和不满的用户。光发得快不够；你得发得好。

Your job is to balance those two forces. Yes, you want your team to move quickly, but not at the expense of building something that doesn’t work. The trick is figuring out how to maintain velocity without sacrificing quality. This might mean tightening up your testing processes or setting clear standards for what “done” looks like so that your team doesn’t ship half-baked features.

你的工作是平衡这两股力量。是的，你希望团队跑得快，但不能以“造出来的东西不能用”为代价。诀窍是搞清楚如何在不牺牲质量的前提下保持速度。这可能意味着收紧测试流程，或者为“完成”设定清晰的标准，好让团队不要把半成品功能发出去。

But there’s a nuance here: quality doesn’t always mean perfection. It’s about knowing when something is good enough to ship and when it still needs work. Great leaders help their teams find that balance, pushing for progress while ensuring what’s delivered actually adds value. Your team needs to trust that when they ship, they’re delivering something meaningful, not just ticking a box.

但这里有个微妙之处：质量并不总是意味着完美。它是知道什么时候东西已经够好可以发、什么时候还需要打磨。伟大的领导者帮助团队找到这种平衡——推动进步，同时确保交付的东西真的增加价值。你的团队需要相信：他们发出去的东西是有意义的，而不只是打了个勾。

Outcomes Aren’t Always Features

结果不总是以功能形式出现

Here’s a common trap: thinking that only the visible work matters. Sure, releasing a shiny new feature feels great, but that’s not the only work that drives outcomes. Sometimes, the most important work your team does isn’t something users will ever see. Infrastructure, technical debt, and internal tools are the silent engines that power the product.

这里有个常见的陷阱：以为只有看得见的工作才重要。的确，发布一个闪闪发亮的新功能感觉很棒，但那不是驱动结果的唯一工作。有时候，团队做的最重要的工作是用户永远看不到的。基础设施、技术债、内部工具，是驱动产品的静默引擎。

It’s easy for teams to lose motivation when they’re working on backend improvements or technical debt that doesn’t get flashy recognition. However, as a leader, your job is to help them see the bigger picture. Explain how this kind of work enables future growth, reduces bugs, and makes everything run smoother. The invisible work is often the most critical, and it’s up to you to ensure your team understands its value.

当团队在做后端改进或技术债、又得不到光鲜的认可时，他们很容易失去动力。然而作为领导者，你的工作是帮他们看到全局。解释这类工作如何为未来的增长铺路、减少 bug、让一切跑得更顺。那些看不见的工作往往最关键，而你有责任确保团队理解它的价值。

It’s about ensuring that the work done today sets the company up for success tomorrow. Celebrate these hidden wins and help your team see that they’re building the foundation for the future.

这关乎确保今天做的工作能让公司在明天取得成功。庆祝这些隐藏的胜利，帮你的团队看到：他们正在为未来打地基。

— 原书第 52 页 —

Exercise: Redefining Your Role for Impact

练习：为影响力重新定义你的角色

In this final exercise, you will define your role as a leader in ensuring that your team delivers outcomes that matter. You will reflect on how to help your team focus on impact, maintain quality while moving fast, and make sure even the invisible work creates real value.

在最后这个练习里，你将定义自己作为领导者在“确保团队交付有价值的结果”这件事上的角色。你会反思如何帮助团队聚焦影响、在快速推进的同时保持质量、并确保哪怕是看不见的工作也创造真实价值。

Step 1: Assess Your Team’s Focus

第 1 步：评估团队的焦点

Start by reflecting on your team’s current reality. Are they creating meaningful impact, or just completing tasks? Write two or three sentences describing where your team stands today in terms of delivering value. Example answer:

先反思团队当下的现实。他们是在创造有意义的影响，还是只是在完成任务？写两三句话描述团队今天在交付价值方面的状态。示例回答：

My team ships code regularly, but they are more focused on hitting deadlines than solving real user problems. We move fast, but quality issues are starting to erode trust.

我的团队定期发代码，但他们更关注赶截止日期，而不是解决真实的用户问题。我们跑得快，但质量问题开始侵蚀信任。

Step 2: Define Your Leadership Approach

第 2 步：定义你的领导方法

Now describe how you will shift your team’s focus from output to outcomes. Write two or three sentences about how you will help them balance speed with quality and make their work count. Example answer:

现在描述你将如何把团队的焦点从产出转向结果。写两三句话，说明你会如何帮助他们在速度与质量之间取得平衡、并让他们的工作真正算数。示例回答：

I will help my team connect their work to customer outcomes, not just tickets closed. We will build habits that protect quality while moving fast, and invest time in the invisible work that keeps our systems strong.

我会帮助团队把自己的工作和客户结果连起来，而不只是关掉的 ticket。我们会养成习惯，在快速推进的同时保护质量，并在让系统保持强健的那些看不见的工作上投入时间。

Step 3: Add to Your Role Description

第 3 步：补充到你的角色说明书

Describe how you will define your role in leading for outcomes. These should describe what you will own as a leader, ensuring quality, managing pace, and reinforcing the value of all work, visible or not. Example answer in April’s context:

描述你将如何定义自己在“为结果而领导”中的角色。这些应描述你作为领导者会拥有什么：确保质量、管理节奏、并强化所有工作（无论可见与否）的价值。April 情境下的示例回答：

At PixelCurl, April’s team has been racing to ship features, but the rush to move fast has resulted in poor-quality code and rising customer complaints. April needs to recalibrate the team’s focus, balancing speed with quality and ensuring that even the invisible work (like infrastructure improvements) is given the attention it deserves. April’s role description could be as follows:

在 PixelCurl，April 的团队一直在赶着发功能，但求快的冲刺导致了低质量代码和不断上升的客户投诉。April 需要重新校准团队的焦点，在速度与质量之间取得平衡，并确保哪怕是看不见的工作（比如基础设施改进）也得到它应得的关注。April 的角色说明书可以是这样：

  • Define success metrics prioritizing impact over output, ensuring that her team’s work drives real value for users and the business. April will guide her engineers to focus on delivering outcomes that matter, rather than just meeting deadlines.

    定义成功指标，把影响排在产出前面，确保团队的工作为用户和业务驱动真实价值。April 会引导工程师聚焦交付有价值的结果，而不只是赶上截止日期。

  • Balance speed with quality, making sure that while the team moves fast, they don’t cut corners that lead to more problems down the road. April will push for velocity, but not at the expense of user experience or product stability.

    在速度与质量之间取得平衡，确保团队跑得快的同时，不会抄近道导致未来出更多问题。April 会推动速度，但不以牺牲用户体验或产品稳定性为代价。

  • Emphasize the importance of invisible work, recognizing that technical debt, infrastructure improvements, and internal tools are essential components of success. April knows that a healthy product needs more than just new features; it requires strong foundations.

    强调看不见的工作的重要性，认识到技术债、基础设施改进和内部工具是成功的必要组成部分。April 知道一个健康的产品需要的不只是新功能；它需要牢固的地基。

— 原书第 53 页 —

By completing this exercise, you will have a clear statement of your leadership focus, guiding your team to deliver meaningful results, maintain high standards, and ensure every line of work adds lasting value.

完成这个练习后，你会得到一份关于自己领导焦点的清晰陈述，它将指引团队交付有意义的结果、维持高标准、并确保每一行工作都增加持久的价值。

We’ll talk more about managing products and shipping in Chapter 6.

关于产品管理和交付，我们会在第 6 章进一步讨论。

Conclusion: Pulling It All Together

结语：把一切串起来

This chapter gave you a comprehensive roadmap for defining your leadership role. From people to mission, planning to process, and finally, outcomes, you’ve dug into the heart of what it means to be an effective engineering leader. You’ve asked the tough questions, reflected on where you are and where you want to go, and translated those insights into an actionable role description.

本章为你提供了一份定义自己领导角色的完整路线图。从人到使命、从规划到流程、最后到结果，你已经挖到了“做一名有效的工程领导者意味着什么”的核心。你问了那些艰难的问题，反思了自己在哪里、想去哪里，并把这些洞察翻译成了一份可执行的角色说明书。

But remember: leadership isn’t static. As your team grows and your company evolves, so will your role. Continue revisiting these questions, refine your approach, and push yourself to lead and inspire.

但请记住：领导力不是静态的。随着团队成长、公司演进，你的角色也会变。持续回头审视这些问题、打磨你的方法，并推动自己去领导、去激励。

In Chapter 3, we’ll dive deep into the diagnostic skills you’ll need to start to navigate the chaos.

在第 3 章，我们会深入探讨你在开始驾驭混乱时所需的诊断技能。
